title: Othello
author: William Shakespeare
about:
Othello is a Moorish general in the service of Venice who has secretly married Desdemona, the daughter of a Venetian senator. His ensign, Iago, has been passed over for promotion and decides to destroy him. Iago insinuates, with no real evidence, that Desdemona is sleeping with Cassio, the lieutenant who got the post Iago wanted. He plants a handkerchief, stages a conversation Othello half-overhears, and works on him until Othello murders Desdemona in their bed. The truth comes out moments after she is dead. Othello kills himself on the same bed.

Shakespeare wrote the play around 1603, drawing on a short Italian novella by Cinthio. Iago repeatedly confides in the audience. We hear him devise an accusation and then see Othello hear it as the reluctant testimony of a friend. The play ran in Jacobean London under the new king James and survived four centuries of debate about who exactly Othello is — Moor, Black African, Berber, soldier, husband, hero, gullible fool — and what Shakespeare meant by putting him at the centre of a love story that ends in a strangling.

Of the four major tragedies, Othello is the most claustrophobic and the most domestic. Venice sends Othello to Cyprus to fight an invasion. A storm destroys the enemy fleet before the armies meet. The action moves from a public council chamber to a married couple’s bedroom.

angleCards.title: Iago's motive.
angleCards.text: Iago gives three different reasons for hating Othello — being passed over for promotion, a rumour that Othello slept with his wife, and pure dislike — and never settles on one. Coleridge called this 'motiveless malignity.' Track what he actually says and decide for yourself.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track every reason Iago gives for hating Othello and decide whether he has a real motive or whether the cruelty is its own end.

angleCards.title: How fast it happens.
angleCards.text: Iago plants the first seed of suspicion in Act 3, Scene 3. By the end of Act 3, Othello is calling for blood. The play is partly an experiment in how quickly a sane, capable man can be talked into murder.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Othello as a study in psychological persuasion: how Iago moves Othello from love to murder in under three hours of stage time.

angleCards.title: Desdemona.
angleCards.text: Desdemona has no flaw the play actually shows. She marries Othello against her father's wishes, defends her choice in front of the Venetian senate, follows him to Cyprus, and protects Othello with her final words when Emilia asks who killed her. Watch what the play does and does not give her.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Desdemona as the play's quietest figure — what she chooses, what she does not get to choose, and how Shakespeare handles a wife who never actually does what she is killed for.

angleCards.title: Race in the play.
angleCards.text: Before Othello arrives, Iago and Roderigo describe him to others through racial and sexual insults. In Act 3 Othello himself says, “I am black,” as he searches for a reason Desdemona might leave him. Compare that moment with the composed way he speaks before the Senate.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Othello with attention to how race functions in the play — what the other characters say about him, what he says about himself, and what the tragedy depends on.

cast.name: Othello
cast.description: A Black general in the service of the Venetian state, recently and secretly married to Desdemona. He has spent his life on campaign, won his place by service, and is the commander the Senate chooses to defend Cyprus. He loves his wife with an intensity that turns into something else the moment doubt enters. The play is the inside of a man who has nothing to fall back on but his honour and is helped to throw it away.

cast.name: Iago
cast.description: Othello’s standard-bearer, passed over for the lieutenancy in favour of Cassio. He confides his schemes to the audience, so we can hear him invent a lie before we see another character believe it. Othello often calls him honest.

cast.name: Desdemona
cast.description: The daughter of the Venetian senator Brabantio, recently eloped with Othello. She is intelligent, brave, and devoted; she defends her marriage in front of the Senate and follows Othello to Cyprus. She does not do, and never considers doing, what Iago accuses her of.

cast.name: Cassio
cast.description: The young officer Othello promotes over Iago at the start of the play. He is charming, educated, and friendly with Desdemona — which is enough, with Iago's help, to make him a target.

cast.name: Emilia
cast.description: Iago's wife and Desdemona's maid. She finds the lost handkerchief and gives it to Iago without knowing what it is for. In the final scene she works out what her husband has done and refuses to be silent about it, no matter what it costs.

cast.name: Roderigo
cast.description: A wealthy Venetian gentleman in love with Desdemona. He pays Iago to help him win her and is strung along through the entire play, used as a knife when Iago needs one and disposed of when he is no longer useful.

acclaim.quote: The picturesque contrasts of character in this play are almost as remarkable as the depth of the passion.
the motive-hunting of a motiveless malignity—how awful it is!
acclaim.context: Note on Act I, scene III, The Literary Remains of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, vol. II

whyItMatters.title: How Iago Makes a Lie Believable
whyItMatters.body: When Cassio leaves Desdemona, Iago only has to say that he dislikes what he has seen. Othello starts asking questions for him. Later Iago lies outright, inventing a story about Cassio speaking of Desdemona in his sleep. He also plants a real handkerchief and arranges for Othello to hear Cassio laugh about Bianca without knowing which woman they mean. The audience can tell an outright lie from an ordinary gesture given a false meaning. Othello comes to treat them both as proof.

whyItMatters.title: The Speed of Belief
whyItMatters.body: Early in Act 3, Othello agrees to receive Cassio at Desdemona’s request. By the end of the garden scene he has knelt to swear revenge, ordered Cassio’s death and begun to plan Desdemona’s. The play compresses what looks, on paper, like an impossibly fast moral collapse into something a sane man can follow scene by scene. Each step Iago takes is small: a question, a reluctance to speak, a half-quoted rumour. Each step Othello takes is just slightly bigger: a worry, then a demand for proof, then a willingness to accept proof too thin. Shakespeare is doing what cognitive psychologists would later call confirmation bias and what con artists have always known: once a man wants to believe something, he will accept evidence he would otherwise have laughed at. The tragedy is not that Othello is stupid. The tragedy is that he is exactly as smart as the rest of us under the same conditions.

whyItMatters.title: Who Gets to Describe Othello?
whyItMatters.body: Iago and Roderigo introduce Othello to the audience with animal comparisons and racial insults before he has a chance to speak. In the Senate, his account of his travels gives us a different measure of him. Desdemona explains what she heard in that story and why she chose him. The Duke supports the marriage but keeps the prejudice alive in a compliment that opposes fairness to blackness. Later Othello reaches for some of the same images as he struggles to explain his fear. In his last speech he asks the survivors to describe him as he is. By then the audience has heard how differently the same man can be described.
